title: Job 3:20–26
context: Job continues to speak and closes his opening lament. He widens the question from his own birth to all who suffer: why is light given to the miserable and life to the bitter in soul, who long for death and do not find it (3:20–22)? He then returns to himself as a man whose way is hidden and whom God has hedged in (3:23), and ends with sighing, groaning, dread realized, and no rest, only trouble (3:24–26). Many readers hear 3:23 as an ironic echo of the protective hedge Satan described in 1:10. Job longs for death but does not seek to bring it about; the chapter is lament, not a suicide text, and it gives sufferers words to bring before God. On how God’s rule relates to evil agents and Job’s losses in the prologue, compare the discussion at Judges 9:23. Job’s friends will begin to answer in chapter 4; the book does not treat their responses as its final word (42:7), and both Arminian and Reformed readers receive this chapter as an honest lament within faith.

verses.text: “Why is light given to him who is in misery, life to the bitter in soul,
verses.arminianNotes: Job widens his question: why is light given to the miserable, and life to the bitter in soul? Arminian readers hear him speaking for all sufferers, not only himself, and stress that God, who gives life and light, does not rebuke honest questions about suffering in the way the friends will.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Job assumes God is the giver of light and life, even while he cannot see why the gift continues in misery. They hold that God’s purposes in suffering, though hidden here, remain good. Shared ground: both traditions read this as a lament question asked before God, not an accusation that ends faith.

verses.text: who long for death, but it doesn’t come; and dig for it more than for hidden treasures,
verses.arminianNotes: Job speaks of those who long for death, but it does not come, and dig for it more than hidden treasure. Arminian readers note that Job describes a longing, not an act; he waits for death rather than seeking to bring it about, and the verse gives honest words to people in deep distress.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Job leaves the timing of death in God’s hands even while he longs for it (compare 14:5). They read the verse as lament from a believer, not a sanction for self-harm. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse pastorally, as voicing anguish that should be brought to God and to others, not acted on.

verses.text: who rejoice exceedingly, and are glad, when they can find the grave?
verses.arminianNotes: Job describes sufferers who would rejoice and be glad to find the grave. Arminian readers hear how deep pain can reverse ordinary hopes, and they stress that God’s care reaches people in that condition; Scripture records such words so that sufferers know they are not alone.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the verse as the honest testimony of how affliction feels, set within a book that moves toward God’s answer and Job’s restoration (42:10–17). They do not take it as Job’s settled judgment on life. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as lament and as a call to compassion toward the suffering.

verses.text: Why is light given to a man whose way is hidden, whom God has hedged in?
verses.arminianNotes: Job asks why light is given to a man whose way is hidden and whom God has hedged in. Many readers hear an ironic echo of the protective hedge Satan described in 1:10. Arminian readers stress that Job does not know of the heavenly scene in chapters 1–2, and that God allowed this testing without willing evil for its own sake.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Job rightly sees God as sovereign over his circumstances, though he cannot see God’s purpose; the hedge that once protected him now feels like confinement. They hold God remained good and wise. Shared ground: both traditions affirm Job’s honesty and that his way, hidden to him, was not hidden to God.

verses.text: For my sighing comes before I eat. My groanings are poured out like water.
verses.arminianNotes: Job says his sighing comes before he eats and his groanings pour out like water. Arminian readers hear the physical weight of grief and note that Scripture takes bodily suffering seriously; God does not ask sufferers to hide their groaning (compare Psalm 6:6; Psalm 102:4–5).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the verse alongside lament psalms where the faithful groan before God (compare Psalm 38:9), seeing groaning as a form of prayer even when it lacks words. Shared ground: both traditions hold that God hears such groaning and that the verse calls readers to patience and presence with those who suffer.

verses.text: For the thing which I fear comes on me, that which I am afraid of comes to me.
verses.arminianNotes: Job says the thing he feared has come on him. Some readers connect this with his care for his children in 1:5, though the text does not say exactly what he feared. Arminian readers stress that Job’s fear was not the cause of his suffering, and that the prologue gives a different explanation (1:8–12).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise reject reading the verse as if Job’s fear brought on his trouble, and note that the prologue grounds his suffering in God’s purposes in the heavenly court. Job’s words describe his experience, not a cause. Shared ground: both traditions hedge any link to 1:5 and decline to blame Job for his losses.

verses.text: I am not at ease, neither am I quiet, neither do I have rest; but trouble comes.”
verses.arminianNotes: Job ends without ease, quiet, or rest, only trouble. Arminian readers note that the chapter closes unresolved, and that Scripture lets this lament stand before God answers (38:1); they stress that the friends who next speak are not the book’s final word on Job (42:7).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the chapter ends in darkness yet within a book that moves toward God’s self-revelation and Job’s restoration (42:1–17). They hold that God’s care did not cease when Job could not feel it. Shared ground: both traditions let the lament stand honestly and wait, with the book, for God’s answer.
